sections.h2: What a transfer on death deed is in Arkansas
sections.html:
Arkansas calls it a beneficiary deed. Ark. Code 18-12-608 defines it as a deed, given without current tangible consideration, that conveys an ownership interest to a named grantee when the owner dies. The deed must say in express terms that it does not take effect until that death.

You will hear it called a TOD deed, a transfer on death deed or a beneficiary deed, but all the rules sit in one code section. The legislature built that section in layers: Act 1918 of 2005, Act 243 of 2007 and Act 570 of 2021.

During the owner's life the grantee holds nothing. Subsection (a)(1)(B) says no legal or equitable interest vests in the grantee until the owner dies without having revoked the deed. The owner keeps control of the house, and the person named has no interest to sell, pledge or claim while the owner is alive.

sections.h2: What the deed must contain to be valid
sections.html:
A valid Arkansas beneficiary deed names the grantee, says it takes effect only at death, and is recorded before the owner dies. Recording is the step that most often decides whether the deed works at all.

  • An express statement that the deed has no effect until the owner's death (subsection (a)(1)(A)).
  • A designated grantee, or several, with the form of co-ownership stated.
  • Recording in the county recorder's office of the county where the property sits, before the owner's death. Under (c)(1), a deed not recorded in time is not valid.
  • For property held as tenants by the entirety or as joint tenants with survivorship, a deed designated by all surviving owners that takes effect at the death of the last survivor (b)(1).
  • Substantial compliance with the statutory form (g).

If fewer than all owners sign, subsection (b)(2) makes the deed valid only when the last surviving owner was one of the signers. Subsection (f)(2) separately preserves a deed that is otherwise effective by law and is recorded only after death. That refers to other kinds of deeds, not to a beneficiary deed.

Use this map to find the exact statutory language before you rely on any summary, this one included.

sections.h2: Who can be named as grantee?
sections.html:
The owner may name one person, several people, a successor or a trustee. The statute is flexible on all four.

  • Several grantees may hold as joint tenants with survivorship, tenants in common, tenants by the entirety, or under any other valid tenancy (a)(2).
  • A successor grantee can be named, including the unnamed heirs of the first grantee, if the deed states the condition that triggers the successor, such as the first grantee not surviving the owner (a)(3).
  • The deed can pass the property to a trustee, including the trustee of a revocable trust, and can name unnamed successor trustees (c)(2).

The tenancy language matters when the house is sold, because a title company will want to know who has to sign. Read it closely before anyone lists the property.

sections.h2: Revoking or replacing a beneficiary deed
sections.html:
An owner may revoke at any time before death by recording a revocation in the same county recorder's office. Subsection (d)(2) requires the revocation to be both signed and recorded while the owner is alive.

Where several owners signed the original deed, any signing owner may revoke. If fewer than all owners sign the revocation, (d)(3) makes it effective only if the last surviving owner signed it and recorded it before that owner's death.

A will cannot undo the deed. Under (d)(4), a compliant beneficiary deed cannot be revoked, altered or amended by the owner's will. When an owner signs more than one beneficiary deed for the same property, subsection (e) gives effect to the one signed last before death, whatever order they were recorded in.

sections.h2: Medicaid recovery against a house passed by beneficiary deed
sections.html:
The state can pursue it. Act 570 of 2021 added language to 18-12-608(a)(1)(B) making the transfer subject to a Department of Human Services claim for reimbursement of federal or state benefits. It also amended section 20-76-436 so the department can claim against the interest a grantee acquires, not only against the estate.

The department's estate recovery rules sort out who is exposed and who is not.

  • People age 55 or older who received long-term care Medicaid in a nursing home or through a home and community-based waiver are covered. Under 55, only people permanently institutionalized.
  • The claim is limited to what Medicaid paid for long-term care, and heirs are not liable above the value of the estate.
  • No claim is made while a surviving spouse is alive, while a child is under 21, or for a blind or disabled child under set conditions.
  • A hardship waiver committee can waive the claim. Factors include whether the home is the sole income-producing asset and whether the home is worth 50 percent or less of the average home price in the county.

Act 570 also gives a grantee a way to ask. When a grantee requests a release or disclaimer in writing, the department has 30 calendar days to assert a claim or provide a disclaimer and release suitable for recording. Where there is no probate, the department sends a demand notice to the county clerk's office and acts if the home is sold.

The deed moves only the real property it describes. Bank accounts, vehicles and other assets still follow a will, beneficiary designations or the small estate procedure.

For small estates, section 28-41-101 lets a distributee collect and distribute property by affidavit, filed with the probate clerk in the right county. The clerk charges $25 to file and $5 per certified copy. The affidavit must say whether the Department of Human Services provided benefits and, if it did, that the department has been reimbursed.

When the estate includes real property, the distributee publishes notice of the death and the affidavit within 30 days of filing, and creditors then have three months from first publication to present claims. That publication step is one reason families sometimes prefer a recorded beneficiary deed for the house itself.

sections.h2: Selling an inherited Arkansas house as a grantee
sections.html:
A grantee who wants to sell first collects the recorded deed, the owner's death record and any department notice, then finds a buyer and schedules a closing. The sale carries the usual transfer tax: $3.30 per $1,000 of actual consideration on transactions over $100, paid by buying a transfer stamp. The Miscellaneous Tax Section at 501-682-7187 handles corrections to a stamp.

Settle these before listing:

  • Whether any mortgage or lien survives, since the transfer is subject to encumbrances made before or after the deed.
  • Whether the department has sent a claim or a demand notice.
  • Whether the deed named several grantees and how they hold title.
  • Whether the house needs repairs a traditional buyer's lender would require.

A cash buyer can purchase the house as it stands once the title questions are answered, with no lender repair list. This page is general information, so an Arkansas attorney or title company should confirm the steps for your deed.

faqs.q: Does an Arkansas beneficiary deed avoid probate?
faqs.a: It moves the named interest at death under the statute's own terms, so the house does not pass under the owner's will. The transfer is still subject to encumbrances and to a possible Department of Human Services claim, and other assets may still need a probate or small estate step.

faqs.q: When must the deed be recorded?
faqs.a: Before the owner dies. Subsection (c)(1) of 18-12-608 requires recording in the county recorder's office where the property is located, and a deed not recorded in time is not valid.

faqs.q: Can an owner change their mind after recording?
faqs.a: Yes. The owner can record a revocation at any time before death, or sign a newer beneficiary deed. If there are several deeds, the one signed last before death is effective, even if another was recorded later.

faqs.q: Can a will cancel a beneficiary deed?
faqs.a: No. Subsection (d)(4) says a compliant beneficiary deed cannot be revoked, altered or amended by the owner's will.

faqs.q: Does the grantee have to sign or accept the deed?
faqs.a: No acceptance is required by subsections (a) through (h) of 18-12-608. The owner signs and records the deed, and the grantee's interest vests only at the owner's death if the deed has not been revoked.
